photos.habitat: Deciduous forests, fields, and woodland edges across eastern North America.
photos.funFact: Box turtles can completely close their shell for protection and have been known to live over 100 years. They have excellent homing abilities and rarely travel far from their birthplace.

photos.habitat: Diverse habitats including forests, fields, wetlands, and suburban areas across North America.
photos.funFact: Garter snakes are among the most cold-tolerant snakes and can be active at temperatures as low as 1°C. They hibernate in large groups called hibernacula.

photos.habitat: Wooded areas with abundant cover such as logs, rocks, and leaf litter across eastern North America.
photos.funFact: Young five-lined skinks have bright blue tails that they can detach if grabbed by a predator. The tail continues to wiggle, distracting the predator while the skink escapes.

photos.habitat: Slow-moving waters with muddy bottoms and aquatic vegetation across North America.
photos.funFact: Painted turtles can survive winter by slowing their metabolism and absorbing oxygen through their skin while buried in mud underwater. They are excellent swimmers and baskers.

photos.habitat: Trees, shrubs, and vegetation in warm, humid areas across southeastern United States.
photos.funFact: Green anoles can change color from bright green to brown depending on temperature, mood, and social signals. Males have a colorful throat fan called a dewlap used for communication.

photos.habitat: Ponds, lakes, marshes, and slow-moving streams across North America.
photos.funFact: Red-eared sliders are excellent swimmers and can hold their breath for up to 30 minutes. They are named for the distinctive red stripe behind their eyes.

photos.habitat: Freshwater swamps, marshes, rivers, and lakes in southeastern United States.
photos.funFact: American alligators are apex predators that can remain motionless for hours. They are excellent mothers, carrying their babies to water in their mouths after hatching.

photos.habitat: Forests, fields, and agricultural areas across southeastern United States.
photos.funFact: Corn snakes are excellent climbers and constrictors. They get their name from the corn-like pattern on their belly scales, not from eating corn.

photos.habitat: Freshwater environments including ponds, lakes, rivers, and marshes across North America.
photos.funFact: Snapping turtles have incredibly powerful jaws and can snap with the force of 208 pounds per square inch. They are surprisingly fast swimmers despite their bulky appearance.

photos.habitat: Arid woodlands, deserts, and scrublands across Australia.
photos.funFact: Bearded dragons can change color to regulate body temperature and communicate. When threatened, they puff out their throat to appear larger and more intimidating.

photos.habitat: Tropical rainforests, mangroves, and coastal areas in Central and South America.
photos.funFact: Iguanas are excellent swimmers and can hold their breath for up to 30 minutes. They have a third eye on top of their head that detects shadows and changes in light.

photos.habitat: Rocky areas, buildings, and urban environments in warm climates worldwide.
photos.funFact: Geckos can walk on any surface, including glass, due to millions of tiny hairs on their feet called setae. They are also one of the few lizards that can vocalize.

photos.habitat: Trees and shrubs in mountainous regions of Yemen and Saudi Arabia.
photos.funFact: Chameleons can move their eyes independently and have tongues that can extend twice their body length. They change color based on mood, temperature, and communication.

photos.habitat: Grasslands, shrublands, and open forests in West and Central Africa.
photos.funFact: Ball pythons get their name from their defensive behavior of curling into a tight ball. They are non-venomous constrictors that can go months without eating.

photos.habitat: Tropical forests, mangroves, and wetlands in Southeast Asia.
photos.funFact: Monitor lizards are highly intelligent reptiles with excellent problem-solving abilities. They are semi-aquatic and excellent swimmers, often diving to escape predators.

photos.habitat: Deserts, grasslands, and scrub forests across southwestern United States and Mexico.
photos.funFact: Rattlesnakes add a new segment to their rattle each time they shed their skin. They can sense heat through special organs and strike with incredible speed and accuracy.

photos.habitat: Tropical and subtropical oceans worldwide, nesting on sandy beaches.
photos.funFact: Sea turtles navigate using Earth's magnetic field and return to the same beach where they were born to lay eggs. They can hold their breath for up to 5 hours.

photos.habitat: Diverse habitats including forests, deserts, and grasslands across North America.
photos.funFact: Kingsnakes are immune to the venom of other snakes and regularly eat venomous species. They are powerful constrictors and excellent climbers.

photos.habitat: Sandy soils in longleaf pine forests and scrub habitats in southeastern United States.
photos.funFact: Gopher tortoises are ecosystem engineers that dig burrows up to 40 feet long, providing shelter for over 350 other species. They are herbivores that help disperse seeds.

photos.habitat: Forests, rocky areas, and swamps across eastern United States.
photos.funFact: Copperheads are venomous pit vipers that can sense heat through special organs. They give birth to live young and are known for their distinctive hourglass-shaped markings.

photos.habitat: Diverse habitats including forests, fields, and rocky areas across North America.
photos.funFact: Milk snakes are harmless constrictors that mimic the coloration of venomous coral snakes. They are excellent rodent controllers and are often found in barns.

photos.habitat: Rocky areas, fences, and open woodlands across North America.
photos.funFact: Fence lizards are excellent climbers and can run on their hind legs when escaping predators. Males have bright blue patches on their throat and belly during breeding season.

photos.habitat: Salt marshes and brackish waters along the Atlantic and Gulf coasts.
photos.funFact: Diamondback terrapins are the only turtle species that lives exclusively in brackish water. They can drink both fresh and salt water through specialized glands.

photos.habitat: Sandy soils in forests, fields, and coastal areas across eastern North America.
photos.funFact: Hognose snakes are master actors that play dead when threatened, complete with rolling over and letting their tongue hang out. They have upturned snouts for digging.

photos.habitat: Grasslands, open woodlands, and scrub areas in southeastern United States.
photos.funFact: Glass lizards are legless lizards often mistaken for snakes. They can detach their tail when threatened, and the tail continues to move to distract predators.

photos.habitat: Streams, rivers, and adjacent forests in northeastern North America.
photos.funFact: Wood turtles are highly intelligent and can be trained to navigate mazes. They have distinctive sculptured shells and are excellent both on land and in water.

photos.habitat: Open areas including deserts, grasslands, and scrublands across southern United States.
photos.funFact: Coachwhip snakes are among the fastest snakes in North America, capable of speeds up to 4 mph. They are excellent climbers and often hunt in trees and bushes.

photos.habitat: Shallow wetlands, bogs, and slow streams in eastern North America.
photos.funFact: Spotted turtles are semi-aquatic and hibernate in mud at the bottom of ponds. Each turtle has a unique pattern of yellow spots that can be used for individual identification.

photos.habitat: Forests, woodlands, and rocky areas with abundant cover across North America.
photos.funFact: Ring-necked snakes are secretive and rarely seen during the day. When threatened, they curl their tail in a corkscrew shape and display their bright orange or red belly.

photos.habitat: Shallow, slow-moving waters with muddy bottoms across eastern North America.
photos.funFact: Musk turtles are also called 'stinkpots' because they release a musky odor when threatened. They are excellent climbers and can often be found basking on low branches over water.
